# In Praise of Traces

There is a stretch of ground in northern Tanzania, near the village of Laetoli, where the earth remembers a walk. Nearly four million years ago, a volcano called Sadiman coughed a plume of ash into the sky, and the ash drifted down over the savanna like gray snow. Then came a light rain—not enough to wash anything away, just enough to dampen the ash into something with the consistency of wet cement. Animals crossed the surface: ancestors of giraffes, three-toed horses, hares, a rhinoceros with a hideously unlucky sense of timing. And then, at some unremarkable moment of some unremarkable day, two hominins crossed it too, moving northward through the ash, leaving behind a trail of seventy-odd footprints along eighty feet of ground before ash and time covered everything and held it, pressed flat, like a flower in a book.

They stayed there for 3.66 million years. In the 1970s, a member of Mary Leakey's archaeological team—by one account he found them during a game of throwing elephant dung at his colleagues, which is the kind of origin story the past seems to enjoy—stumbled onto the prints. When the overburden was brushed away, the trail read almost like a sentence. Here was an arched foot, a proper heel strike, a big toe pointing forward: creatures already committed to walking upright, long before anyone could have explained to them why this would matter. Two tracks run side by side, one distinctly larger than the other, with strides that match, which some interpreters have taken to mean companions—a parent and child, or two friends. A few writers have even ventured that at one point the pairs of prints seem to pause, to turn toward each other, though the evidence is too soft to carry that much weight. Still, the temptation is understandable. Two figures, side by side, walking through falling ash: it is hard not to invent the conversation.

I think about those prints a lot, and about what they represent, which I'd call, provisionally, a trace: the mark left behind by a passage, the residue of matter having touched matter. Almost everything that happens in the universe evaporates instantly, leaving no evidence it occurred. A trace is the exception—a slight drag on total forgetting. And the older I get, the more I suspect that traces are not incidental to the world but fundamental to it, that reality has a habit of keeping receipts, and that nearly everything we know about anything is built on this habit.

Start with the sky. We go through our days under the pleasant illusion that light is instantaneous, that seeing is a kind of present-tense acquaintance with things as they are. It isn't. Light travels fast, but it travels, and everything we see arrives late. The Moon shows you how it looked a second and a quarter ago. The Sun you feel warming your face on a spring morning is an image dispatched eight minutes before it touches you—and that is only the last leg of the journey. A photon born in the Sun's core takes, by some estimates, a hundred thousand years of ricocheting off charged particles before it reaches the surface and finally accelerates into open space. The sunlight on your skin is therefore a double trace: light that is minutes old, forged from events older than our species. Look further and the lag grows astronomical. The Andromeda galaxy, faintly visible from a dark hillside, presents itself as it was two and a half million years ago, around the time those hominins were treading ash in Tanzania. When a massive star dies in a supernova, its light can arrive for weeks, months, centuries—sometimes the star is entirely gone and its news keeps coming anyway, like a letter that arrives after the writer's death. Astronomy, in this light, isn't really the study of distant objects. It is archaeology. Every telescope is a shovel turned toward the deep strata of time, and the dig is ongoing everywhere you point your eyes.

Down here on Earth, traces accumulate more modestly but no less relentlessly. Touch the banister of an old building and you're touching wood polished by ten thousand palms before yours. Climb the worn steps of an ancient cathedral and notice how the stone has hollowed into shallow bowls, each depression the aggregate of half a million feet. Brass door plates thin invisibly at the height of a hand. On university quads, neat paved walkways lose arguments to the desire paths—those dirt streaks students wear diagonally across the grass—which record, better than any committee minute, where people actually want to go; and it is said that many of our oldest city streets began exactly this way, as footpaths worn stubbornly into mud centuries before anyone surveyed them. Forensic science has codified the whole phenomenon. Its founding insight, usually credited to the criminologist Edmond Locard, is that every contact leaves a trace: fiber, hair, soil, oil from a fingertip. Walk through a room and the room changes because you did. The claim sounds mystical put that baldly, but it is merely the physics of surfaces, and it means that innocence and guilt alike are written continuously into the world, whether anyone intends to write or not.

Nature keeps archives of its own, patient and methodical. Tree rings record each year's feast and famine, so that a dendrochronologist can read the drought diary of a forest across a thousand years, counting backward from the bark to the year the rains failed. Glacial ice traps bubbles of ancient atmosphere as it forms, so that cores drilled from Antarctica hold actual samples of Ice Age air—the breath of a vanished world, still pressurized, still extractable, sixty times older than agriculture. Sediment settles into strata like pages lying one atop another; strike a cliff face anywhere and you're thumbing a geological book whose chapters run to millions of years apiece. Even lightning leaves documents: where a bolt strikes sand, the current can fuse the grains into a branching glass tube called a fulgurite, a lightning strike converted literally into mineral, an instant hardened into an heirloom.

Human history rides on this same physics, which is both consoling and embarrassing. Consoling, because without it we would know nothing whatsoever about our origins; embarrassing, because what we know arrived almost entirely by accident, according to no principle worth defending. Consider the strange survival of the world's oldest written complaint. Around 1750 BCE, a merchant named Ea-nasir operated in the Sumerian city of Ur, dealing in copper. A customer named Nanni, dissatisfied with the quality of Ea-nasir's goods and his attitude besides, had his grievance pressed into a clay tablet—the famous complaint tablet, now sitting serenely in the British Museum, immortalizing a transaction dispute that outlasted the Akkadian, Babylonian, Assyrian, Persian, Greek, Roman, Ottoman, and British Empires all stacked on top of it. Meanwhile, essentially every song sung, every speech delivered, every prayer whispered, and every dream confided by the millions of ordinary people across those same forty centuries vanished completely, in most cases within a generation of being uttered. History is not a record of the past. It is the sack of odds and ends the past happened to drop on its way out the door—and we sort through the wreckage calling it knowledge.

The ancients understood, dimly or keenly, that permanence can't be commanded. Kings raised monuments specifically engineered to ensure remembrance, and time handled those promises roughly: pyramid casings quarried away for other buildings, bronze inscriptions melted for scrap, statues decapitated by weather or piety. Often the humbler leavings prove more eloquent than the grand designs. Kitchen middens teach archaeologists what people ate; scratched school exercises on broken pottery show how children learned; a coal seam from a hearth tells you a Tuesday happened in a particular hut in a particular winter. Intentions do not control legacies. The universe accepts submissions and then files them wherever it likes.

Sometimes a trace preserves not just existence but feeling, and this is where things get tender and strange. In Chichester Cathedral in England lies a stone tomb commissioned in the late fourteenth century for Richard FitzAlan, Earl of Arundel, and his wife Eleanor. Their effigies lie side by side, and their right hands are joined—not clasped in a formal pose but interlinked, gently, fingers threaded. Whether this was the earl's instruction or Eleanor's, or the sculptor's flourish, or a courteous guess by a later restorer of damaged stone, nobody knows. In 1955, Philip Larkin stood in front of the tomb, started to turn away out of boredom, and felt himself "unstrengthened by" what he saw—or seen by it. His poem, "An Arundel Tomb," circles the ambiguity with characteristic distrust and then surrenders to it anyway, arriving at the line that has followed the tomb ever since: "Our almost-instinct almost true: / What will survive of us is love." Larkin hedged—"almost," he says twice in one line, a poet refusing to be caught in sincerity—but the stone did what stones occasionally manage. Across six hundred years, an uncertain gesture persuaded a skeptic to write a sentence strangers now say at weddings. The trace did its work.

Writing itself began as trace-keeping in the most literal sense. The earliest writing we possess, from Mesopotamia, is not scripture or poetry but accounting—tallies of grain, beer, livestock, debts. Civilization's first instinct upon inventing notation was to keep receipts, which should temper anyone's romanticism about the human spirit while also explaining a lot about the human spirit. And once writing existed, its makers couldn't resist slipping traces of themselves into it. Medieval copyists, bent over parchment by candlelight for twelve hours a day, left a genre of involuntary autobiography in their margins: complaints about thin ink and bad pens, notes about cold hands and aching backs, exclamations of relief at finishing a section, occasional curses aimed at the cats. Several surviving manuscripts contain actual cat paw prints stamped between the lines of text where some animal sauntered across still-wet ink—and at least one scribe seems to have drawn a tolerant little picture memorializing the intrusion. Margins fill with doodles: knights battling snails, rabbits with alarming weapons, faces peering out of initial letters. These professionals of preservation spent their lives producing documents intended to transmit serious texts to the future, and the future, characteristically, is most charmed by their accidents. There may be a lesson there. Posterity, when it eventually reads us, will care less about what we meant to say than about our paw prints.

Which raises an uncomfortable modern paradox. For most of history, the constraint on tracing was the medium: even clay, the great preservative, had to be lucky—though, satisfyingly, when conquerors burned the libraries of Mesopotamia, the flames accidentally fired and thus hardened the clay tablets, so that warehouse receipts from Ur now outlast the poetry of Alexandria. Our era inverted the problem. Stone and paper are passive; they sit in archives getting older but remaining themselves. Digital information is not stored so much as constantly rehearsed—it exists only insofar as machinery keeps rewriting it into fresh substrates. Stop migrating it, refreshing it, paying the electricity bill, and it doesn't decay gracefully into accessible ruin; it becomes noise, indistinguishable from nothing. Hence a delicious humiliation now legend in archival circles: the Domesday Book, William the Conqueror's census of England, compiled in 1086, remains perfectly readable today, while its commemorative multimedia successor, produced in 1986 with state-of-the-art laser discs and custom software, became effectively unreadable within a decade and a half. Nine hundred years of technological advantage, thoroughly beaten by sheepskin. Computer scientists now warn seriously about a digital dark age—an unprecedented situation in which the best-documented generation in history may become the least retrievable one. We are drowning in traces and preserving almost none of them durably. The scribes at least knew their materials would outlive them. We pay monthly fees and trust marketers.

At the same moment, a second anxiety arises from the opposite direction: the impossibility of not leaving traces. Laetoli's walkers moved through unowned ash, witnessed by nothing but falling debris, free in the deepest sense—no record, no reputation, no file. We cannot take a step outdoors without cameras logging coordinates, phones announcing location, sensors tasting the air of our presence. Entire industries exist to correlate our trails. Predictably, a counter-desire has arisen with almost spiritual force: the wish for tracelessness. Leave No Trace ethics among hikers treat an unmarked wilderness passage as a small sacrament. Privacy advocates argue that the right to move through the world without shedding legible residue is not paranoia but dignity—an old-fashioned insistence that some moments belong only to the moment. Even here the truth refuses simplicity, since those same accumulated traces save lives daily: a watch that detects the arrhythmia, a mapping database that reroutes an ambulance. We resent the exhaust of our data and depend on its engine. Being traceable and wanting privacy, we inhabit the contradiction without resolution.

But zoom out, and even the resentments dissolve into something like awe. Eighty-odd light-years from Earth, a spherical shell of radio waves is expanding outward at the speed of light—a sphere containing television broadcasts, telephone calls, radar pings, the ambient static of our century, all of it information shed from our species the way the body sheds skin. It is the largest footprint humanity has made. Whatever form it eventually reaches—itself dimming, leaking, gradually encrypted by distance into obscurity—it is proceeding on schedule, requiring from us no maintenance, no subscriptions, no migration to newer formats. Physics, indifferent patron of archives, accepted the submission. Someday, in principle, somewhere, those waves arrive at somebody's instrument, and a receptionist of another biosphere straightens up in whatever passes for a chair.

And maybe that's the honest consolation at the bottom of all this. At Laetoli, the rain fell on the ash, the ash received two sets of footprints without consulting anyone, and time set the plaster forever without asking permission or announcing its plan. None of the walkers knew. They were doing the most ordinary thing in the world, and the world quietly decided it was worth keeping. There is every reason to believe our lives work the same way—that each of us presses hourly into surfaces we can't see, our casual gestures drying into sediment whose future legibility is not ours to determine. Most traces will wash out. A handful won't, and there's no formula for which handful. All we can do is what the Laetoli pair apparently did: proceed, together or apart, step after ordinary step, meanewhile building the only record that has ever really mattered to anyone else—the accumulated pressure of having been here, passing through.

Even this essay is one: words pressed down in a certain order by a certain pressure of attention, meeting, now, another pressure—that of your eyes moving across them. Two trails, briefly parallel. The shorter of us walks beside the taller, for a page or two, out of sight by now to both of us—

but not, perhaps, out of the ground.
